# Setting up the SRA Toolkit {#sec-setup}

The **SRA Toolkit** is NCBI's set of command-line programs for SRA data. You
need three of them: `prefetch` (download), `vdb-validate` (check) and
`fasterq-dump` (convert to FASTQ). This chapter gets them installed and
configured on whatever computer you have: a laptop, a lab workstation, or a
shared cluster.

## Where should you run this?

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
  Q1{"How much data?<br/>(add up the Bytes column)"} -->|"a few runs,<br/>< ~50 GB of .sra"| L["Laptop or workstation<br/>with ~20x that free on disk"]
  Q1 -->|"many runs, or<br/>more than you have disk for"| Q2{"Do you have a<br/>computing cluster?"}
  Q2 -->|yes| C["Cluster: run in its<br/>scratch space, as batch jobs"]
  Q2 -->|no| W["Workstation with a large<br/>external or network drive,<br/>or download from ENA in chunks"]
```

| Requirement | Why |
|---|---|
| macOS or Linux (Windows: use **WSL**, the Windows Subsystem for Linux) | The toolkit and the scripts here are command-line tools |
| **Free disk space ~10–20× the `.sra` size**, while converting | `fasterq-dump` writes large temporary files ([details](fasterq-dump.qmd#disk-space)) |
| A few CPU cores (4–8) | `fasterq-dump` is multi-threaded |
| A stable internet connection | Downloads of many GB |

## Install: pick one option

### Option 1: conda (recommended; any Mac or Linux)

[conda](https://docs.conda.io/) installs bioinformatics software into an
isolated *environment* without needing administrator rights. If you don't
have it, install [Miniforge](https://github.com/conda-forge/miniforge) first.

```bash
conda create -n sra -c conda-forge -c bioconda sra-tools pigz
conda activate sra          # do this in every new terminal
fasterq-dump --version
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Apple Silicon Macs (M1/M2/M3/M4)

If conda says a package isn't available for your platform, create the environment
for Intel Macs, which runs through Rosetta:

```bash
CONDA_SUBDIR=osx-64 conda create -n sra -c conda-forge -c bioconda sra-tools pigz
```
:::

### Option 2: NCBI's prebuilt binaries

From the [SRA Toolkit install page](https://github.com/ncbi/sra-tools/wiki/02.-Installing-SRA-Toolkit):

```bash
## Linux (Ubuntu build; an AlmaLinux build is also available)
wget --output-document sratoolkit.tar.gz \
  https://ftp-trace.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra/sdk/current/sratoolkit.current-ubuntu64.tar.gz
## macOS
curl --output sratoolkit.tar.gz \
  https://ftp-trace.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra/sdk/current/sratoolkit.current-mac64.tar.gz

tar -vxzf sratoolkit.tar.gz
export PATH=$PWD/sratoolkit.3.*/bin:$PATH     # add this line to ~/.bashrc or ~/.zshrc to keep it
which fasterq-dump
```

### Option 3: your cluster's module system

Most university clusters already have the toolkit installed as an
**environment module**:

```bash
module avail sra            # look for sra-tools, sratoolkit, or similar
module load <name>/<version>
fasterq-dump --version
```

Prefer a 3.x version. Older 2.x versions have bugs and lack options used here.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## On UNC Longleaf

`module avail sra` lists the toolkit. Run downloads in your `/work` space
(`/work/users/<first letter>/<second letter>/<onyen>/`), inside an interactive job
(`srun -p interact -n 1 -c 6 --mem=8g -t 4:00:00 --pty bash`) or with `sbatch`,
never on the login node. Copy finished `.fastq.gz` files to your lab's `/proj`
space, because `/work` is purged.
:::

## Check it works

NCBI's own test fetches two reads from a small run and prints them:

```bash
fastq-dump --stdout -X 2 SRR390728
```

You should see eight lines of FASTQ. If it hangs or errors, see
[Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd).

## Configure it (once)

The toolkit keeps settings in `~/.ncbi/user-settings.mkfg`, edited with
`vdb-config`.

### Where downloads go

Depending on configuration, `prefetch` saves into the **current directory**
or into a **user repository** under your home folder (e.g.
`~/ncbi/public/sra`). On a laptop that may be fine. On a cluster, home folders
are usually small, and a full home breaks everything else. The predictable
choice everywhere: save to the current directory, and `cd` to a folder with
space before downloading.

```bash
vdb-config --prefetch-to-cwd
```

(Or run `vdb-config -i`, open the **TOOLS** tab, and set the location there.)

### SRA Lite or Normalized {#sra-lite-or-normalized}

`vdb-config -i` opens an interactive screen. On its main page there is an option
**"Prefer SRA Lite files with simplified base quality scores"**
([what that means](databases.qmd#whats-in-an-.sra-file)):

- **Unticked** (prefer Normalized, full qualities): the safe choice if you'll
  look at quality plots or quality-trim.
- **Ticked**: smaller downloads, constant quality 30.

Move with the arrow keys or the highlighted letters, toggle with space, then
**Save** and **Exit**.

::: {.callout-note}
Newer toolkit versions may ask you to run `vdb-config -i` once before the first
download, even if you change nothing: open it, save, exit.
:::

## A folder layout that works anywhere

```bash
mkdir -p ~/public_data/GSE52778 && cd ~/public_data/GSE52778   # or a scratch/external drive
mkdir -p sra tmp fastq logs
```

```
GSE52778/
├── SRR_Acc_List.txt     # runs to download
├── SraRunTable.csv      # metadata
├── sra/                 # .sra files from prefetch (deleted after conversion)
├── tmp/                 # fasterq-dump temporary files
├── fastq/               # the .fastq.gz you keep
└── logs/
```

On a cluster, put this in the **scratch** space (large and fast, but usually
not backed up), and copy `fastq/` and the metadata somewhere permanent when
you're done.
